faq.a: Lightning heats the air around it to about 30 thousand degrees Celsius, roughly five times hotter than the Sun's surface. The air expands explosively, sending out a shock wave we hear as thunder.
asks: Why does lightning make a noise?

faq.q: Why does thunder rumble for so long?
faq.a: A lightning bolt is kilometres long, and sound from each part of it reaches you at a different time. The bangs from near and far parts, plus echoes, blend into a long rumble.
asks: Why is thunder a long sound?

faq.q: Why does nearby thunder crack but far thunder rumble?
faq.a: Close up you hear all the sound, including sharp high-pitched parts, as a loud crack. Over long distances air absorbs the high pitches, so only low rumbles reach you.
asks: Why is close thunder so sharp?

faq.q: How far away can you hear thunder?
faq.a: Usually up to about 15 kilometres, depending on wind, hills and background noise. If you can hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck by lightning.
asks: Can thunder be heard 20 km away?

faq.q: Can there be lightning without thunder?
faq.a: No, all lightning makes thunder. But if the storm is very far away, the thunder fades before it reaches you, so you may see silent flashes.
asks: Why do I see lightning but hear nothing?

facts: Lightning can heat the air to about 30,000 degrees Celsius, around five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Thunder can usually be heard up to about 15 kilometres from a lightning strike.
